text:
I take the use-domain cases as stipulated. I do not have the original construction, source packet, or supplemental criticism, so I do not rely on the returned account’s historical claims about P7, P9, C0, WHL, RSS, etc. I use the returned account only where it supplies a relevant formal distinction: local alternatives versus aggregation, independent versus constrained aggregation, and conditional compatibility criticism. I qualify its “locus” language as descriptive rather than as a new target category.

## Case A

The reporting specification is arithmetic: subtract the sum of selected quantities from capacity and return the integer.

Selected quantities: K has 6, L has 5.  
Sum: \(6+5=11\).  
Capacity: 9.  
Reporting result: \(9-11=-2\).

So the reporting result is \(-2\). What follows is that, under the reporting specification, the selected entries sum to 11 reservation units, which exceeds the stated capacity of 9 by 2 units. Because each booking has exactly one selected entry, and there are no ties, releases, or expired holds, there is no other selected quantity in the file that changes this arithmetic.

But a negative result does not by itself prove that either hold is invalid, that K and L cannot be jointly performed, or that the file is erroneous. A stronger conclusion—say, “this file is over-allocated and infeasible under capacity”—needs an additional premise such as: capacity is a hard upper bound on the sum of selected active holds; the holds must be simultaneously satisfiable; and no other adjustment, release, or offset is relevant. Without that premise, the only secure conclusion is the specified arithmetic one: selected quantities exceed capacity by 2.

Under the returned account’s formal framework, Case A can be treated as two singleton local alternatives, \(A_K=\{6\}\) and \(A_L=\{5\}\), combined by a simple aggregation rule that subtotals and subtracts from capacity. The compatibility criticism discussed below is not activated by any supplied inspection in Case A. Any stronger claim about the selected entries would require an added aggregation or capacity assumption.

## Case B

The snapshot lists:

- U alternatives: \(0\) or \(8\)
- V alternatives: \(0\) or \(11\)
- capacity: \(23\)

The reporting procedure forms every pair \((u,v)\) and displays \(23-u-v\).

| U | V | \(u+v\) | \(23-u-v\) | Inspection feasibility |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 23 | jointly performable |
| 0 | 11 | 11 | 12 | jointly performable |
| 8 | 0 | 8 | 15 | jointly performable |
| 8 | 11 | 19 | 4 | not jointly performable |

So the specified reporting procedure returns:

\[
\{23,\;12,\;15,\;4\}
\]

including the pair \((U=8,V=11)\), whose arithmetic value is \(23-8-11=4\).

With the inspection file available, the pair \((U=8,V=11)\) cannot be performed jointly because both need the same single-use jig at the same time. Each of the other listed pairs can be performed jointly. Therefore the planner’s requested values, restricted to jointly performable pairs, are:

\[
\{23,\;12,\;15\}
\]

If the planner wants an annotated table rather than a filtered set, the entry \((8,11)\) still has arithmetic value 4, but it is marked infeasible. If the planner asks only for values of jointly performable pairs, 4 is excluded.

A reader who has only the snapshot and reporting procedure, without the inspection file, can support the following:

- The listed local alternatives are \(U\in\{0,8\}\) and \(V\in\{0,11\}\).
- The reporting procedure forms all four pairs.
- The arithmetic outputs are \(23,12,15,4\).
- All four arithmetic outputs are nonnegative; no listed pair exceeds capacity under the simple sum \(u+v\).
- If capacity were the only relevant cross-booking constraint, all four pairs would remain within capacity.

That reader cannot support:

- that all four pairs are jointly performable;
- that \((8,11)\) is impossible;
- that the planner’s feasible value set is exactly \(\{23,12,15\}\);
- that no unnamed physical-resource constraint matters.

The reader can say “the reporting procedure outputs these four values.” The reader cannot say “these four values are exactly the feasible planner-usable availability values” without an extra premise that the Cartesian product of local alternatives equals the joint feasibility relation, or that capacity is the only cross-booking constraint.

## The reviewer’s remark before inspection

The reviewer wrote:

> “Each listed quantity may be defensible on its own, yet a pairing might fail to be jointly performable. A resource that the snapshot does not name might matter.”

At the time it was made, before the inspection file, this is a conditional compatibility criticism. It challenges the step from “U=8 is listed and V=11 is listed” to “the pair \((8,11)\) is jointly performable,” or more generally from “each booking’s alternatives are locally defensible” to “any choice of one alternative per booking can be composed into a global feasible state.” In the returned account’s vocabulary, it challenges an aggregation rule or a source assumption inside that rule: the assumption that local alternatives combine independently except for named constraints such as capacity.

It does not challenge the listed quantities themselves. It explicitly allows that each listed quantity may be defensible on its own. It does not supply a different quantity for U or V. It does not identify any actual impossible pair. It does not by itself show that the snapshot is wrong. It says that the snapshot’s silence about physical resources is not sufficient to prove that no such resource matters.

Where it affects an account is at the aggregation/use step. If an account treats the product of local alternatives as exact global availability, or as planner-usable availability, then the remark says that claim is under-supported. If the account presents the product merely as an arithmetic enumeration of listed pairs, or as an outer enclosure under an explicit independence assumption, then the remark requires no mathematical change; it requires a qualification.

There are defensible alternative readings of the remark:

1. **Weak epistemic caveat.** “Might” means only that the snapshot underdetermines joint feasibility. No actual unnamed resource is known. Under this reading, nothing changes in the quantities or the arithmetic; only overclaiming is blocked.

2. **Strong actual-defect reading.** The remark suggests there really is some unnamed resource that matters, so the independent product overgenerates. By itself, however, the remark supplies no observed resource and no identified impossible pair. It becomes concrete only when something like the inspection file identifies the jig conflict for \((8,11)\).

3. **Source-completeness reading.** The remark challenges the snapshot as an incomplete source for joint feasibility. It does not challenge the local quantities or the calculation; it says a resource/compatibility model or inspection is needed before the product can be used as planner-usable feasibility.

The inspection file distinguishes the weak and strong readings for this finite case. It supplies an actual resource conflict: U=8 and V=11 need the same single-use jig at the same time. That makes the strong reading true for the pair \((8,11)\) after the inspection. A case in which all listed pairs can be performed jointly would leave the weak caveat true but the strong reading false. A case in which a shared resource exists but is not needed simultaneously would also fail to produce the conflict.

Does anything in the remark alone require changing a listed quantity or the reporting calculation? No. It supplies no observed resource and no identified impossible pair. It may require changing a claim about what the calculation means—for example, do not call the four reporting values “exact feasible planner values” without further support. But the listed quantities remain 0 or 8 for U and 0 or 11 for V, and \(23-u-v\) remains the same arithmetic expression for each pair.

## Relation to the returned account

The returned account’s local/aggregation distinction maps directly onto Case B. The local alternatives are

\[
A_U=\{0,8\},\qquad A_V=\{0,11\}.
\]

The reporting procedure uses independent aggregation:

\[
F_{\text{ind}}=A_U\times A_V,
\]

and computes

\[
\operatorname{Av}_{\text{ind}}=\{23-u-v:(u,v)\in F_{\text{ind}}\}
=\{23,12,15,4\}.
\]

The inspection file supplies a constrained feasibility relation:

\[
F=F_{\text{ind}}\setminus\{(8,11)\},
\]

so the planner’s feasible values are

\[
\operatorname{Av}_F=\{23-u-v:(u,v)\in F\}
=\{23,12,15\}.
\]

The returned account’s compatibility criticism is exactly the reviewer’s remark formalized: if an unnamed cross-booking constraint makes some product combination impossible, then treating \(F_{\text{ind}}\) as exact global feasibility overgenerates. The account’s “when change is required” passage also fits: if the account claims exact or planner-usable availability, then it must add a joint feasibility/resource model, weaken to an outer enclosure, or decline to give a usable global answer. If it merely reports arithmetic over all listed pairs, no mathematical change is required.

I use the returned account’s passages defining the local component, aggregation component, constrained aggregation, compatibility criticism, and the conditions under which change is required. I do not rely on its historical P7/P9/C0/WHL/RSS claims, because those materials are not supplied here. I also qualify the “locus” terminology: it is useful descriptively to say the compatibility criticism bites at the aggregation step, but it need not be treated as a new kind of target beyond the aggregation rule or source assumption.

There is a real tension, but not a contradiction, between the four reporting values and the three planner-feasible values. The reporting procedure forms every listed pair and computes \(23-u-v\); that yields 4 for \((8,11)\). The planner asks only for jointly performable pairs; the inspection excludes \((8,11)\), so the planner’s set omits 4. The unresolved issue is whether the reporting procedure was intended as exact feasible availability or merely as an arithmetic enumeration over listed pairs. If it was intended as exact feasible availability, then after the inspection it should be qualified, annotated, or filtered. If it was merely arithmetic over all pairs, it remains \(\{23,12,15,4\}\). That distinction should be stated rather than resolved by silently dropping 4 or by pretending the reporting procedure already knew the jig constraint.
